20:20 This guy is awesome. "I think we should have the same vision [for] the future." That's spot-on. Arguing about the past is futile. We mustn't _forget_ the past, but we can't remain stewing in it, angry and intolerant. I wish nothing but the best for these lovely folks moving forward.

One of my best friends is a Bosniak who, along with his brother and mother, were smuggled out of the region into Austria, then Germany. He was about 14 years old, and at the time he didn't know where his father was, or if he was even alive. Thank God his father wound up living through the war and eventually found his wife and sons. 

My friend is one of the most intelligent, perceptive, and hilarious people I've ever met. We met at work in ~2004 and he taught me everything I know about Bosnia and the wars. Our jobs were at an international airport and they employed many, many Balkan refugees. I worked there for ~13 years and knew dozens of Serbs, Croats, and Bosniaks. I'm rambling like hell. Division between peoples fkn bums me out. Especially religious division.

comments.author: @tomgu1988
comments.text: Great video, but I realized something as a Bosnian Serb. If we are being completely honest and strip away all the modern political complexes and nationalistic narratives on the Balkan peninsula, our daily lifestyle, mentality, and cultural DNA are actually much closer to the Levant than to Western Europe.Western Europe—like Germany or Scandinavia—is built on strict individualism, emotional restraint, and a rigid separation of family and work. In contrast, the Balkans and the Levant share a fundamentally collectivist culture. For us, family always comes first, hospitality is an unwritten law, and our concept of time is relaxed and fluid. Our daily life revolves around sitting for hours over coffee, and our culinary traditions (from Sarma and Ćevapi to Baklava) reflect centuries of shared history. Even our music, like Turbo-Folk or Sevdalinka, utilizes the same melancholic microtones and emotional intensity that you find in the Middle East. When a Balkaner experiences "Dert" or "Merak," a Lebanese or Syrian understands that feeling instantly, while a Western European might just see it as a lack of discipline.The reason why I write this is because I realized in this video that Bosnian Muslims, in particular, often try to distance themselves from the Middle East by aggressively labeling themselves as "strictly European." They often say, "We are different from Arabs because we are European," but what they actually mean is simply that they live a secular lifestyle. They are confusing deep cultural, social, and emotional roots with how religious they are.Furthermore, the Levant is not a monolithic religious block; it is a highly diverse, historically cosmopolitan region with its own secular and multi-faith realities. Using "Europe" as a civilizational shield to look down on the East is just a coping mechanism for a regional inferiority complex.Ultimately, if you put a Balkaner in Frankfurt, they might understand the administrative system, but they often feel isolated by the "cold" culture. But if you place that same Balkaner—whether Serb, Bosniak, or Croat—in a living room in Beirut or Damascus, they will instantly feel at home because the warmth, the volume, the food, and the social dynamics are completely familiar. We are the bridge between the West and the Orient, and we shouldn't use "Europe" as a tool for cultural arrogance or elitist gatekeeping.

You've got one half trying to abolish the other half, you've got one ethnic group having its member of presidency be elected by another ethnic group, you've got the colonial governer and the continued regime of not having full sovereignety only being supported by the largest ethnic group because the Bosniaks and the international representatives effectively function as a single voting bloc and, last but not least, you've got every single issue possible endlessly politicized as the three groups constantly try to gain the upper hand over each other: from holidays, to police reform, to literally just about everything else.
